question: What is the main job of vitamin D made in the skin?

options.A: Preventing ultraviolet radiation damage to cells
options.B: Eliminating excess urea through sweat glands
options.C: Assisting with calcium absorption in the body
options.D: Regulating core body temperature during a fever

explanation: Great job! Sunlight on the skin helps create vitamin D, which your body needs to properly absorb calcium for strong bones and teeth. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h1)

question: How does your skin help cool you down on a very hot day?

options.A: By constricting surface blood vessels to trap heat
options.B: By shedding the outer epidermal layer to release trapped heat
options.C: By increasing subcutaneous fat thickness to block external warmth
options.D: By producing sweat and widening blood vessels near the surface

explanation: You've got this! Sweat cools you as it evaporates, and widening your blood vessels lets warm blood flow close to the surface so heat can escape. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h1)

question: Which skin layer is found only in thick areas like the palms of your hands and soles of your feet?
explanation: Spot on! The stratum lucidum is a clear, extra protective layer found only where we experience heavy friction, like our palms and soles. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h2)

question: Why do the cells on the very outer layer of your skin not have nuclei?

options.A: They have been damaged by direct exposure to ultraviolet radiation
options.B: They are specialized immune cells that do not require genetic material
options.C: They are actively dividing stem cells that have temporarily discarded their DNA
options.D: They are dead, keratin-filled cells that have been pushed upward from deeper layers

explanation: Exactly right! As skin cells travel up from the bottom, they flatten, fill with tough keratin, lose their nuclei, and form a protective dead layer. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h2)

question: What type of tissue mainly makes up the deeper part of the dermis (the reticular layer)?
explanation: You nailed it! This tough tissue is packed with collagen fibers that give your skin strength and help it resist tearing when stretched. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h3)

question: If someone gets a deep scratch that damages their dermal papillae, what unique skin feature is affected?

options.A: The storage of subcutaneous fat for insulation
options.B: The synthesis of active vitamin D from sunlight
options.C: The production of protective keratin proteins
options.D: The formation of unique fingerprints and friction ridges

explanation: Well done! The dermal papillae push up into the upper skin layer to create the ridges that form our unique fingerprints and help us grip things. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h3)

question: What is the main type of tissue found in the hypodermis (the layer right under the skin)?
explanation: Correct! The hypodermis is mostly made of adipose (fat) tissue, which keeps us warm, stores energy, and cushions our organs. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h4)

question: Why is the hypodermis so important for protecting your bones and muscles?

options.A: It contains active stem cells that repair bone fractures
options.B: It acts as a physical shock absorber against trauma
options.C: It generates sweat to cool deep tissues during exercise
options.D: It produces keratin to harden the surface against impacts

explanation: Spot on! The layer of fat cushions bumps and blows, protecting the delicate muscles and bones underneath. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h4)

question: Which skin gland makes an oily substance called sebum to keep your hair and skin soft?
explanation: You're doing great! Sebaceous glands are our natural oil glands, usually attached to hair follicles, keeping our skin waterproof and moisturized. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h5)

question: What causes 'goosebumps' on your skin when you feel cold or frightened?

options.A: Contraction of tiny arrector pili muscles attached to hair follicles
options.B: Overproduction of watery sweat by widespread eccrine glands
options.C: Rapid constriction of blood vessels within the papillary dermis
options.D: Swelling of the stratum corneum due to moisture absorption

explanation: Exactly! Tiny muscles attached to your hair follicles pull them upright when you're cold, creating those little bumps on your skin. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h5)

question: Which skin receptor is especially good at sensing deep pressure and fast vibrations?
explanation: Spot on! Pacinian corpuscles are deep in the dermis and act like tiny sensors for strong pressure and vibrations. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h6)

question: When you accidentally touch something very hot and pull your hand away instantly, which nerve endings feel that pain?
explanation: Well done! Free nerve endings reach up into the skin to act as our alarm system for pain and temperature changes. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h6)

question: What does a bluish color in a patient's skin (cyanosis) usually mean?
explanation: You've got it! Cyanosis happens when there isn't enough oxygen in the blood, giving the skin and lips a bluish tint. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h7)

question: When a nurse gently pinches the skin to check hydration (skin turgor), which fibers in the dermis make the skin snap back?
explanation: Brilliant! Collagen and elastin give the dermis its spring and flexibility, helping nurses quickly check if a patient is well-hydrated. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T1#GNS213_U5_T1_h7)
